group.passage:
On weekdays, they must get up early in the morning. Equipped with whistles, batons, and traffic signs, they must put on luminous jackets, yellow armbands, and peaked caps as well. At busy intersections, they escort pedestrians to pass the crossroads safely and avoid turning vehicles. Hailed as the unsung heroes for road-crossing children in primary schools, they are crossing patrols, or more fondly known as the “lollipop men and women” in the UK.
The first lollipop lady in England is said to be Mary Hunt, a school caretaker who voluntarily aided pupils in Bath to reach the class in 1937. The crossing patrols were not paid until the late 1940s, when the number of lollipop men began to soar. As these traffic management personnel came to be widely adopted, the government enacted “The London Traffic Law” in 1952 to endow them with legal authorities. Drivers in London who did not stop as instructed would be fined £5 for trespassing. With the rising awareness about road safety, the “Road Traffic Regulation Act” in 1967 further extended the enforcement from London to the entire Britain.
In the 1950s, the stop signs used by crossing patrols were black-and-white rectangles fixated on a pole. The round sign that looks like a lollipop as we see today, with the word “STOP” on a horizontal black strip and an international symbol for schoolchildren, was introduced in the early 1960s. Before long, the term “lollipop men” was first used by a fictional character, a young boy named Charlie, in a play meant to tour around schools for road safety. Since the mid-1960s, crossing patrols in the UK have been nicknamed “lollipop men and women.”
In their heyday, there are 7,128 lollipop men and women officially employed by councils. Local authorities tend to recruit retired gentlemen as the patrollers with a modest salary, but in recent years, some begin to cut the funding for financial reasons. Now in the UK, there are less than 2,000 lollipop men in total.

figures.caption: 第1題四個選項皆為黑白線條插圖
figures.description: 四幅黑白卡通線條插圖，由左至右為選項(A)–(D)。(A) 一輛校車的正面，擋風玻璃上方的牌子寫著「SCHOOL BUS」，駕駛座上坐著一位戴高帽、面帶微笑的司機。(B) 一名穿著多口袋工作服、戴有帽簷帽子的男子，一手高舉槌子（斧頭狀工具），一手提著工具箱，作走路狀。(C) 一名穿條紋反光背心（夾克）、戴有帽簷帽子的男子站在馬路上，一手持長桿，桿頂是寫著「STOP」的圓形標誌（字下方另有小圖示），另一手高舉示意；他身後兩名背書包的學童正走在斑馬線上過馬路。(D) 一名留八字鬍、戴帽子的男子站在一台有輪子的推車攤旁，推車上方撐著一把大型條紋陽傘，推車上擺有器具（街頭攤販）。

questions.stem: Which of the following is the closest illustration of a lollipop man?

options.A: ［圖］一輛校車的正面：擋風玻璃上方有「SCHOOL BUS」字樣，駕駛座上坐著一位戴高帽的司機。
options.B: ［圖］一名穿著多口袋工作服、戴有帽簷帽子的男子，一手高舉槌子（斧頭狀工具），一手提著工具箱。
options.C: ［圖］一名穿條紋反光背心、戴有帽簷帽子的男子，手持長桿頂端寫著「STOP」的圓形標誌、另一手舉起示意；身後兩名背書包的學童正走在斑馬線上過馬路。
options.D: ［圖］一名留八字鬍、戴帽子的男子站在一台有輪子的推車攤旁，攤車上方撐著一把大型條紋陽傘（街頭攤販）。

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT the reason why British government made laws for lollipop men?

options.A: Mary Hunt was injured when she was on duty.
options.B: There were more and more lollipop men in Britain.
options.C: Lollipop men needed legal power to perform their duties.
options.D: British people put greater emphasis on the importance of road safety.

questions.stem:
In what time order did the following items appear?
a. the term “lollipop man” coined by a playwright
b. crossing patrols using lollipop-shaped signs
c. crossing patrols using square traffic signs
d. salary given to crossing patrols
What can we infer from the last paragraph?

options.A: Females are denied the access to being lollipop men.
options.B: The prospect of lollipop men in Britain is dim.
options.C: The aging population is a potential threat for road safety.
options.D: Councils should hire more young people as lollipop men.
